summary: Defines a generic way for IKEv2 to use any of several symmetric secure password authentication methods. It adds no new method, but provides a way to agree on which method to use and a common way to carry method-specific payloads. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6467 gives IKEv2 peers a common way to choose among secure password authentication methods and exchange the messages each method needs. It defines a framework, not a new authentication method.

questions: how to negotiate secure password method
what is the ikev2 secure password framework

subtitle: A shared negotiation and message format for secure password methods in IKEv2.

tldr.problem: Several secure password authentication methods for IKEv2 used different negotiation procedures and payload formats, making it difficult for one implementation to support multiple methods.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Notify payload to select one method during IKE_SA_INIT and a generic payload to carry method-specific data during IKE_AUTH.
tldr.outcome: The framework allows different secure password methods to share a common IKEv2 structure, but it defines no new password method itself. It is Informational.

today: RFC 6467 is an Informational RFC published in December 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it defines the IKEv2 secure password framework, not a specific password method.

sections.title: Why a Common Framework Is Needed
sections.content:
Several secure symmetric password methods were being developed for IKEv2. Their earlier drafts used different ways to negotiate the method and different message formats, making it difficult for one implementation to support more than one.

RFC 6467 provides common formats for selecting a method and carrying the data specific to that method. It does not define a new secure password authentication technique. The RFC describes use between peers that share a secret, such as servers or routers; it says these methods are not generally aimed at ordinary remote-access users, for whom EAP-based authentication may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Different password methods needed a shared way to identify themselves and exchange their messages. This RFC provides that shared structure, while separate specifications define each method.

sections.title: Selecting a Method During IKE_SA_INIT
sections.content:
The secure password method must be selected during IKE_SA_INIT because the methods may change the later IKE_AUTH exchange. The initiator sends a Notify payload listing acceptable secure password method identifiers. The responder selects exactly one method and includes that choice in its response.

Each method identifier is a 16-bit number assigned by IANA. If the Notify payload is absent, the peers use normal IKEv2 authentication methods. Selecting a method early lets later exchanges use a single agreed method rather than negotiating separately in every method-specific message.
sections.plainLanguage: At the start of the exchange, the initiator lists the password methods it can use. The responder selects one method, and both peers use that method in the next stage.

sections.title: The Generic Secure Password Payload
sections.content:
The Generic Secure Password Method (GSPM) payload carries data required by the selected method. Its payload type is 49. The framework does not define the contents of that data; the individual password method defines its own format and may define subtypes inside the payload.

A common payload avoids assigning a separate IKEv2 payload type to every method. A method can send one or more GSPM payloads during IKE_AUTH, depending on its requirements. The selected method is not repeated in each GSPM payload because the peers already chose it during IKE_SA_INIT.
sections.plainLanguage: After choosing a method, the peers use one shared payload type to carry that method's data. The method's own specification defines the contents of those messages.

sections.title: How the IKE_AUTH Exchange Uses the Payload
sections.content:
During IKE_AUTH, the initiator and responder exchange identity and security-association information along with the GSPM payloads required by the selected method. If the method needs several rounds, the peers exchange additional IKE_AUTH messages containing more GSPM payloads.

The method defines how its data contributes to the final AUTH calculation. RFC 6467 assigns authentication method number 12 for generic secure password authentication, and the IKEv2 payload registry assigns payload type 49 to GSPM.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers exchange the selected method's messages during IKE_AUTH. When authentication finishes, the method also defines how its data is included in the final authentication check.

sections.title: Security and Registry Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6467 does not define an exact authentication protocol, so it does not specify the security properties of a particular password method. A method that uses these payloads must describe its own security properties.

The RFC allocates a Notify message type for secure password method negotiation, an IKEv2 authentication method number for the generic method, and the GSPM payload type. It also creates a registry for method numbers, with later changes handled through Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: This framework carries messages but does not make a password method secure by itself. Each method specification must explain the protection it provides.
